title: Hasselback Potatoes
subtitle: Swedish fanned roast potatoes
excerpt: Each potato is sliced almost all the way through at 3mm intervals, brushed generously with butter, and roasted until the tips are crisp and the inside is fluffy. Named after the Hasselbacken restaurant in Stockholm, these give a far better crisp-to-soft ratio than ordinary roast potatoes.
sourceNotes: Hasselback potatoes are named after the Hasselbacken restaurant in Stockholm, where they were created in the 1950s. Each potato is sliced almost all the way through in thin layers, which fan out during roasting to give crisp edges and a soft centre.

content.text: The trick is placing each potato between two wooden spoon handles or chopsticks on the chopping board. They act as guides and stop the knife cutting all the way through. Slice at 3mm intervals across the width and you get the classic fanned shape.
Place each potato on a chopping board between two wooden spoon handles or chopsticks. Slice down at 3mm intervals across the width -- the spoon handles stop the knife cutting all the way through.
Arrange in a roasting tin. Brush all over with melted butter, getting some into each slit. Season with salt and pepper.
Roast for 45 minutes. Remove and brush again generously with butter. Press breadcrumbs into the slits.
Roast for a further 15 minutes until the tips are crispy and golden.

items.cause: Not brushed with enough butter or oven not hot enough
items.fix: Brush again generously and raise the oven to 230°C for the final 10 minutes.

content.text: Sweden. An invention of the Stockholm restaurant scene in the 1950s. Now popular worldwide as a more elegant roast potato. The fanned shape gives a much better crisp-to-soft ratio than a whole baked potato.
